title: The Home Computer Arrives
tagline: Beige computers, cassette tapes and a phone the size of a brick.

locale.persona: a teenager in a suburban family with a new home computer

morningRoutine.detail: Home computers like the Commodore 64, launched in 1982 at $595, started straight into BASIC.
The Walkman personal cassette player, on sale since 1979, made music personal and portable.

places.title: The front page
places.description: 1984 brought a new kind of computer, the break-up of the national phone monopoly and the Los Angeles Olympics.
places.imageAlt: A 1984 front page about a new computer and the Olympic Games
highlights: The Bell System is broken up
Los Angeles hosts the Summer Olympics

futureVisions.prediction: Cyberspace: "a consensual hallucination experienced daily by billions of legitimate operators, in every nation."
futureVisions.note: The novel popularised "cyberspace"; the internet and online communities followed.

source.label: Computing History (UK): Novelist William Gibson invents the term cyberspace

futureVisions.prediction: Touch screens and compact discs will become everyday ways to use and store information, with computers in kiosks and in the hands of children.
futureVisions.whoSaidIt: Nicholas Negroponte, talk at the first TED conference, February 1984
futureVisions.note: Touchscreen phones, CD-ROMs and service kiosks all arrived, as TED's own summary of the talk notes.

source.label: TED: Nicholas Negroponte, "5 predictions, from 1984" (TED1984, February 1984)

futureVisions.prediction: Information wants to be free, because the cost of getting it out is getting lower and lower all the time.
futureVisions.whoSaidIt: Stewart Brand, at the first Hackers Conference, 1984
futureVisions.note: Copying and sending information now costs almost nothing, though the fight over paying for it never went away.

source.label: Campus Technology, May 2005: 'Information wants to be free' (quotes Brand at the 1984 Hackers' Conference)
